name: 5th Sunday of Easter
description: The Way, the Truth, and the Life. The Vine and the Branches.
biblicalBasis: Jesus' farewell discourse: "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser... Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me" (John 15:1-8). The commandment of love: "Love one another as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:12-13).
significance: The vine and the branches is the strongest image of the fellowship between Christ and believers—without connection, there is no fruit. To "abide in" Christ is not a mystical escape from the world but practical love. The commandment to love is not a new law but a consequence of being connected to Him who is love itself.
liturgicalContext: White color. The theme of the farewell discourse characterizes the Sundays leading up to Ascension—Jesus prepares His disciples for His absence and the coming of the Spirit.
history: The vine as an image of God's people is pervasive in Christian art and theology. The Church Fathers (especially Augustine) used the vine metaphor as a key text to explain the necessity of grace and the fruitfulness of faith.
otConnections: Israel as God's vineyard in Isaiah 5:1-7—the vineyard that bore no fruit. Psalm 80:9-16 about the vine God planted from Egypt. Hosea 10:1 about Israel as a fruitful vine. Jesus is the "true" vine—the fulfillment of what Israel was meant to be.

references.reason: The day is about abiding in Christ and bearing fruit. The text that a tree is known by its fruit, and that a good tree bears good fruit, is a direct parallel to the vine and the branches (John 15), which is the main theme of the day.
